e.t: This Hebrew name refers to “Assyria,” the land and power repeatedly named in the Old Testament. It functions as a proper name, identifying Assyria rather than describing a general quality or action. The word occurs 151 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Zechariah, and is especially prominent in the historical books and Isaiah. Its uses include references to Assyria in relation to kings, nations, commands, giving, and conflict.

“Shimites” is a group name for people identified by this Hebrew word. It functions as a noun naming a people rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears two times, in Numbers 3:21 and Zechariah 12:13. The English rendering “Shimites” preserves its function as a people-name, while the exact identity of the group is understood from the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

This Hebrew verb means “cleave,” describing something split or separated into parts. In the Old Testament, it is used especially for animals whose hoof is divided, and for the action of tearing or splitting. It occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, chiefly in Leviticus and Deuteronomy, where divided hooves help identify animals under Israel’s dietary instructions. The same basic idea can describe physical separation in other passages. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being divided or torn.

This Hebrew word means “poured” and refers to the act or result of something being poured out. It functions as a concise description of pouring rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both occurrences appearing in Leviticus 4:12. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic sense remains connected with something being poured.

Tahath is a Hebrew proper name, rendered consistently as “Tahath.” It identifies a named entry rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. The name occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Numbers and 1 Chronicles. Because the available material does not include the surrounding verse text, it does not establish whether each occurrence refers to a person, place, or another named subject. Its stable rendering supports treating Tahath as a name, while the precise identity in each passage must come from its immediate context.

This Hebrew word refers to “heaviness,” describing a burdened or weighty condition. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra 9:5. Since the available wording identifies the basic idea but does not provide the surrounding verse text, the word should be understood at the lexical level rather than assigned a more specific emotional or spiritual meaning. Its precise force in Ezra depends on how the surrounding passage uses the idea of heaviness.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of being “strong.” It functions as a describing word, presenting a person, thing, or power as possessing strength rather than weakness. It occurs five times in the Old Testament, in Ezra and Daniel, with four occurrences in Daniel. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary sense is a description of strength and capability.

This word means “Baharumite,” a designation identifying a person by association with Baharum. It is not a general description of an action, quality, or object, but a personal or geographical designation. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs only once, in 1 Chronicles 11:33. The available rendering consistently gives “Baharumite,” so that is the supported meaning without adding further details about the individual or the place. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.
